\chapter{An Ancient Cousin and a Second Emigrant}
\label{ch:rot-blau}
\hlchaptermodality{21}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say red and blue in German, and say which of them Romance borrowed.}

The second half of the same argument, with a twist in each colour. rot is Germanic raudaz and goes back to one of the oldest reconstructable colour words -- and Latin ruber is its COUSIN rather than its source, so the resemblance is inheritance from far enough back that neither borrowed. blau is the second emigrant: Germanic blewaz went into French as bleu, and English then borrowed its own blue back from French rather than keeping the word it had inherited.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[rot]{rot — \textquotedblleft{}red\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-rot}



\begin{quote}
You have black and white. The next colour is not a matter of taste — languages the world over reach for the same one third.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: rot}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{rot} — \textquotedblleft{}red.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Three letters, one syllable, and very close to the English word underneath the spelling.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{long-o} — the \emph{o} is \textbf{long}, the vowel of English \emph{road}, not the short \emph{o} of \emph{rot}. The German word does not rhyme with the English word spelled the same way.
  \item \texttt{d-t-final} — the closing \emph{t} is crisp and fully released: \emph{roht}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{culture}
If a language has only two colour words, they are dark and light. If it has a third, it is \textbf{red} — before green, before blue, before yellow. That holds across unrelated families on every continent, which is why \emph{schwarz}, \emph{weiß} and \emph{rot} are the three this chapter and the last one reach for first.

Blood and fire are the guess most people make, and it may be right; what is certain is the order, not the reason.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rot\textquotedblright{} — long \emph{o}, as in \emph{road}
  \item the three in order — \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, weiß, rot\textquotedblright{}
  \item the warning — \textquotedblleft{}rot does not rhyme with English \emph{rot}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}rot, rot — roht.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}red.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Rot}.) Is the \emph{o} long or short? (\textbf{Long} — as in \emph{road}.) Which colour do languages name third? (\textbf{Red}.) And the first two? (\textbf{Dark and light} — black and white.) Next: the cousin it has in French, and why it is not a borrowing.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rot, red, rouge]{rot, taken apart}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-rot-ruber}



\begin{quote}
The last lesson had a German word the Romance languages borrowed. This one has a German word they did \textbf{not} borrow — and they have it anyway.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Rot} comes from Germanic *\emph{raudaz}, and behind that from Proto-Indo-European *\emph{h\textsubscript{1}rewd\textsuperscript{h}-} — one of the oldest colour words that can be reconstructed at all. It went everywhere:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{what it became} \\
\midrule
German & \textbf{rot} \\
English & \textbf{red}, and \emph{rust}, \emph{ruddy} \\
Latin & \emph{ruber}, \emph{rubeus} — and so French \textbf{rouge}, plus \emph{ruby}, \emph{rubric} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

So \emph{rot} and \emph{rouge} are \textbf{cousins, not borrowings}. They did not pass from one language to the other; they split apart thousands of years before either language existed, and each walked its own road to a word for red.

That is a different relationship from the one \emph{blank} has with \emph{blanc}. There, a word crossed a border within recorded history. Here, two words inherited the same ancestor and never met again.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the family — \textquotedblleft{}rot, red, rouge\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English extras — \textquotedblleft{}rust, ruddy\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two relationships — \textquotedblleft{}blank and blanc: borrowed. Rot and rouge: cousins.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}rot, red, rouge.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which French word is \emph{rot}'s relative? (\emph{\textbf{Rouge}}.) Did French borrow it from German? (\textbf{No} — they are cousins.) Which Latin word is in the line? (\emph{\textbf{Ruber}}.) Name two English words from the same root besides \emph{red}. (\emph{\textbf{Rust}}, \emph{\textbf{ruddy}}.) Next: the fourth colour, which \textbf{was} borrowed.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[blau]{blau — \textquotedblleft{}blue\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-blau}



\begin{quote}
The fourth and last colour of the set — and the second one German lent abroad.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: blau}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{blau} — \textquotedblleft{}blue.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Four letters, one syllable, and the vowel is the trap.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-au} — German \emph{au} is the vowel of English \emph{house} or \emph{cow}. It is \textbf{not} the \emph{aw} of \emph{law} and not the \emph{oo} of \emph{blue}.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{blau} rhymes with English \textbf{cow}: \emph{blow} as in \emph{plough}, never \emph{blow} as in \emph{blew}.

That one vowel is what stops an English speaker recognising the word by ear even though it is the same word.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}blau\textquotedblright{} — rhyming with \emph{cow}
  \item the wrong one, then the right one — \textquotedblleft{}not \emph{bloo} … \emph{blau}\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four — \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, weiß, rot, blau\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}blau, blau — rhymes with \emph{cow}.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}blue.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Blau}.) Which English word does it rhyme with? (\emph{\textbf{Cow}}.) Does it rhyme with \emph{blue}? (\textbf{No}.) Say all four colours. (\textbf{Schwarz, weiß, rot, blau}.) Next: the journey this word took, and the odd route English used to get it back.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[blau, bleu, blue]{blau, taken apart}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-blau-bleu}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Blank} emigrated. So did this one — and then English did something strange to get it back.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Blau} comes from Germanic *\emph{blēwaz}, and like \emph{blank} before it, this word was \textbf{borrowed into Romance}:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}blue\textquotedblright{}} \\
\midrule
German & \textbf{blau} \\
French & \textbf{bleu} \\
Italian & \textbf{blu} \\
English & \textbf{blue} — taken from \textbf{French}, not from Germanic \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read that last row twice. English is Germanic. It had inherited *\emph{blēwaz} itself — the word was already sitting in Old English — and it borrowed the French form anyway.

So the word went \textbf{Germanic $\to$ French $\to$ English}, and arrived home wearing Romance clothes. English \emph{blue} is a German word that took the long way round and is no longer recognisable as one — which is exactly why \emph{blau} does not sound like \emph{blue}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Portuguese went somewhere else entirely: its blue is \textbf{azul}, from \textbf{Arabic}. One colour, and within a few hundred miles you can find a Germanic word, a Germanic word laundered through French, and an Arabic one.

Colour words travel more than almost any other kind, because they are easy to borrow: you can point at the thing. Verbs and grammar stay home; the names of shades move with cloth, dye and trade.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the family — \textquotedblleft{}blau, bleu, blu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the long way round — \textquotedblleft{}Germanic, French, English\textquotedblright{}
  \item the outlier — \textquotedblleft{}azul, from Arabic\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}blau, bleu, blue — one word, three stops.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two German colour words did Romance borrow? (\emph{\textbf{Blank}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{blau}}.) Where did English get \emph{blue} from? (\textbf{French} — not directly from Germanic.) Which language's blue is Arabic? (\textbf{Portuguese} — \emph{azul}.) Next: all four colours, and what each of them did.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — four colours, four histories}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-rot-blau}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Four colours, and no two of them got where they are the same way.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{source} & \textbf{did Romance take it?} \\
\midrule
\emph{schwarz} & Germanic *\emph{swartaz} & no \\
\emph{weiß} & Germanic *\emph{hwītaz} & no — but \emph{blank} went instead \\
\emph{rot} & Germanic *\emph{raudaz} & no — Latin had its \textbf{own} cousin \\
\emph{blau} & Germanic *\emph{blēwaz} & \textbf{yes} — \emph{bleu}, \emph{blu} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Four native Germanic words and not a Latin borrowing among them, which is worth saying plainly: German did not get its colours from Rome. Two of them went the other way.

And the \textquotedblleft{}no\textquotedblright{} in row three is a different kind of no from the ones above it. \emph{Schwarz} and \emph{weiß} stayed home. \emph{Rot} has a Romance relative anyway — because Latin inherited the same ancient word rather than borrowing the German one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all four — \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, weiß, rot, blau\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two traps — \textquotedblleft{}rot as \emph{road}, blau as \emph{cow}\textquotedblright{}
  \item the cousins that prove the family — \textquotedblleft{}rot · red · rouge\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two that emigrated — \textquotedblleft{}blank, blau\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, weiß, rot, blau.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Run the four colours. How many were borrowed from Latin? (\textbf{None}.) Which two did Romance take from German? (\emph{\textbf{Blank}} \textbf{and} \emph{\textbf{blau}}.) Is \emph{rouge} a borrowing from \emph{rot}? (\textbf{No} — a cousin.) Which English colour word came home through French? (\emph{\textbf{Blue}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
